chunks.text: The kadamba is a fast-growing evergreen tree of the coffee family, Rubiaceae, native across southern China, the Indian subcontinent and much of Southeast Asia, capable of reaching 45 metres with a broad crown and a straight cylindrical trunk, and notable among tropical hardwoods for extremely rapid early growth in its first six to eight years. It produces dense, ball-shaped, sweetly fragrant orange-red flower heads about 5.5 centimetres across, maturing into a fleshy compound fruit carrying thousands of tiny wind- and rain-dispersed seeds, and its relatively soft, pale wood, while not prized for strength, is widely used for plywood, pulp and paper, packing crates and dugout canoes because it is fast to grow, easy to work and simple to treat with preservatives. Its deepest cultural resonance is with Krishna: the Bhagavata Purana and widespread North Indian devotional tradition place Krishna and Radha playing in the shade of a kadamba tree on the banks of the Yamuna, and one well-known episode has Krishna climbing into its branches to tease the gopis bathing below by making off with their clothes. In South India the same tree instead carries the title 'Parvati's tree', underscoring how a single species can anchor quite different regional mythologies within one broader Hindu tradition, and it is further honoured as the designated city tree, or sthala vriksha, of Madurai, where a preserved relic specimen stands within the Meenakshi Amman Temple complex. Historically, the Kadamba dynasty that ruled from Banavasi in present-day Karnataka between the fourth and sixth centuries CE took its name directly from the tree and treated it as sacred, and the tree's flowers are also recorded, in the classical Kama Sutra, as something lovers playfully pelted one another with — a small but telling detail of how deeply the species was woven into everyday cultural life well beyond temple ritual.

chunks.source: Ugaoo (horticulture retailer) knowledge centre — Growing Kadamba, Lord Krishna's Favourite Tree
chunks.text: Aimed at Indian home gardeners around the Janmashtami festival season, this practical growing guide reinforces the tree's devotional associations — repeating that Krishna is said to have played his flute and performed the Raas-Lila in the kadamba's shade with Radha, and noting the tree's place among the nakshatra trees traditionally planted together in astrological gardens — while also giving basic cultivation notes aimed at people wanting to grow one themselves: propagation is by seed sown in grow bags during the monsoon and transplanted out the following rainy season, the tree wants well-drained soil and a humid climate, and it is notably frost-sensitive, with even established, mature trees capable of being killed back to ground level by a hard frost. It describes the mature tree as large and fast-spreading, often exceeding 10 metres with a wide crown of big, glossy, dark leaves and drooping branches, flowering in the rainy season with the same sweet-scented, globe-shaped blooms described in more technical sources, and bearing round fruit that lingers on the tree long enough to draw both birds and fruit bats. It also notes, in passing, that extracts of the bark and leaves have a place in Ayurvedic preparations, and that the flowers are valued commercially as a raw material for Indian attar perfume — practical, present-day confirmation of uses otherwise described mainly in historical or mythological terms elsewhere.
